title: Heartbeat gap gambit and fallback design scratchpad
content:
Summary:

We experienced a transient observability outage on 2025-11-02 where synthetic heartbeats from multiple regions dropped to 0 in the central metrics store for ~18 minutes. That silence cascaded into false-positive SLO burn alerts and triggered multiple on-call escalations. This doc is a working scratchpad capturing the on-call timeline, quick mitigations, root-cause hypotheses we exercised, and a proposal for a concrete fallback/runbook pattern to prevent similar cascades.

Why this matters:
- Synthetic heartbeats are a sentinel input to routing and SLOing for several services (api-gateway, model-serving, dedupe layer). When heartbeats vanish, automated systems start to (a) mark systems as unhealthy, (b) shift traffic, and (c) open escalation paths.
- The root failure was not service downtime — it was metrics delivery and aggregator behavior. That means user-facing services were mostly healthy, but wide downstream churn happened anyway.

Incident timeline (UTC):
- 2025-11-02 09:02: Gateway synthetic pings for eu-west-1 first observed 30-40% drop in ingestion.
- 09:04: SRE pager fired: multiple services reporting heartbeat missing for >2 minutes.
- 09:06: Ops pulled prometheus-exporter logs — increased 5xxs from exporter to central collector.
- 09:10: Central metrics collector (pulling job) started returning 429s for a subset of scrape targets.
- 09:12: On-call: rotated through restart of collector pod (did not materially change 429s).
- 09:15: Short-term mitigation: disabled high-cardinality debug exporters (manual toggle) to reduce collector load.
- 09:18: Heartbeat ingestion recovered to ~96%. SLO alerts started to auto-resolve by 09:35.

What we observed during triage:
- Collector returned intermittent 429s correlated with bursts of high-cardinality metrics posted after a deploy in infra/telemetry earlier the same morning.
- The collector's internal in-memory series map hit eviction behavior (LRU) under memory pressure; lower-QPS, high-priority synthetic heartbeat series were sometimes dropped and later re-registered, creating a prolonged gap in contiguous samples (which our alerting rules interpreted as downtime).
- Exporters were still up; they reported successful post attempts but many responses were throttled. Network egress and infra were nominal.

Hypotheses we validated quickly:
1) "Rate-limit induced series eviction": validated by correlating collector 429 windows with spike in unique series cardinality. Confirmed.
2) "Exporter misconfiguration caused payload blowup": one newly-deployed debug exporter included full request headers as labels, increasing cardinality per host. Confirmed in rollout PR #482.
3) "Alerting rule sensitivity": our heartbeat alerting rule is binary: no samples for N minutes -> page. This amplifies transient ingestion gaps into pages. Confirmed through simulation.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Rollback / toggle of the debug-exporter change via toggle API (owner: telemetry team).
- Temporary raise of collector rate-limits and ephemeral CPU/memory bump for the collector cluster to absorb backlog (owner: infra).
- Short-term change to alerting: increase heartbeat missing window from 2 minutes to 5 minutes and add a 'recovery smoothing' silence for auto-resolved alerts to avoid duplicate pages (owner: eng-sre).

Why existing defenses failed:
- Rate-limits were global and did not prioritize synthetic heartbeats over high-cardinality debug metrics.
- Collector lacks a lightweight backpressure signal to exporters that would allow them to shed labels or sample less frequently instead of retrying and escalating cardinality.
- Alerting rules were too brittle for ingestion-layer issues (they assumed signal loss = service outage).

Runbook draft: "Heartbeat ingestion degradation" (short checklist for on-call)
1) Verify service health: confirm upstream services report healthy (k8s pod status, app logs) to avoid conflating service outage vs telemetry gap.
2) Check collector status page and scrape error rates (prometheus job: collector/scrape_errors, 5xx rate, 429 windows).
3) If 429s present: identify recent deploys to telemetry/infra in the last 60 minutes (check CI/deploy timeline).
4) Toggle high-cardinality debug exporters off (toggle location: /telemetry/toggles, owner: telemetry team).
5) If toggles not available: temporarily block suspicious targets via collector config (blacklist rule) to reduce cardinality and preserve sentinel series.
6) Apply temporary alert leniency (increase missing-window) and silence duplicate pages.
7) Scale collector horizontally if capacity allows.
8) After recovery: capture full scrape traces and collector mem/series metrics; file artifact in incident ticket and proceed to RCA.

Small sample Prometheus queries helpful in triage:
- collector_429_count_total{job="collector"} by (instance)
- sum by (job)(rate(telemetry_scrape_errors_total[1m]))
- count by (metric_name) (telemetry_series_active{job="collector"})
- topk(20, increase(telemetry_series_created_total[5m]))  # spot cardinality bursts

Longer-term remediation proposals (owner + rough ETA):
A) Prioritized ingress lanes (owner: infra/telemetry) - 2–3 quarters
- Implement priority buckets in the collector: mark sentinel series (synthetic heartbeats, SLI metrics) as high-priority and never evict them under memory pressure.
- Expose a lightweight HTTP backpressure header so exporters can switch to a low-cardinality mode (drop optional labels, sample less).

B) Cardinality safety net (owner: telemetry) - 1 quarter
- Add an admission control layer that rejects label explosions per-tenant per-minute and returns a structured 429 with suggested mitigation (e.g., "shed-labels=1").
- Emit explicit telemetry for "label-shed events" for future automation.

C) Alerting robustness (owner: eng-sre) - 1 month
- Change heartbeat alert rule to: missing for M minutes AND collector_scrape_error_rate < threshold OR heartbeat_bucket_rate < threshold. In short: combine ingestion health checks with the absence of signal to reduce false positives.
- Add a short automatic suppressor window for resolved pages coming from ingestion gaps.

D) Safer deploys for telemetry code (owner: dev-experience + telemetry) - next sprint
- Require cardinality check in CI for any telemetry/metrics changes; block PRs that increase unique series above baseline by X%.
- Add a pre-merge smoke test that exercises the collector at low scale with synthetic high-cardinality payload to detect blowups.

Open action items (concrete):
- SRE-1245: implement collector priority lanes + sentinel list (owner: Priya, infra) - status: in triage.
- OBS-332: CI cardinality gate for telemetry repos (owner: Maya) - status: ready for sprint planning.
- SRE-1246: refine heartbeat alerting rule + implement auto-suppress behavior (owner: Ravi) - status: in progress.
- GH PR #482: telemetry debug exporter change - follow-up to land stricter label sanitization (owner: Sofia) - status: merged (hotfix rolled back then fixed).

Notes / design tradeoffs to discuss:
- Priority lanes reduce false positives but introduce risk of metric starvation for low-priority signals — we need to define an emergency degradation policy rather than a binary keep/evict.
- Backpressure headers require exporter changes across many internal services; consider a phased approach starting with the biggest cardinality generators.
- CI cardinality gates will add friction to telemetry iteration; aim for conservative defaults and an override path for emergency debug deploys with proper guardrails.

Quick checklist for next on-call rotation (what to check in the morning):
- collector_429_count_total[1h] for spikes
- increase(telemetry_series_created_total[30m]) topk(50)
- recent deploys to telemetry in last 2h (CI dashboard)
- heartbeat_missing_alerts: any recurring flapping in past 24h

Appendix: short reproducible scenario to test locally
- Run a small collector instance via docker-compose with collector config limited to X series and a mock exporter that emits 50k unique series over 2 minutes. Validate eviction and sentinel preservation behavior after implementing the priority-lane patch.

Concluding thoughts (scratchpad):
This incident sits at the intersection of instrumentation hygiene, collector policy, and alerting logic. Fixes are both engineering (priority lanes, backpressure) and behavioral (CI gates, deploy discipline). The runbook draft above is intended to be short and practical for on-call; if it proves effective we should formalize it in Confluence and include the triage queries as a standard page.

-- ravi
